pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Preventing erosion (comparing design solutions)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1/KS2 working scientifically — perform simple comparative tests; design & technology evaluate solutions):** Pupils compare ways to slow or stop wind and [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-1] and judge which works best from evidence.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-ESS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-1].

- **Operational details:** This is an early ENGINEERING-design / comparison node. Children first grasp that wind and water erode land (carry soil away), then examine and COMPARE solutions that reduce it — plants/ground cover (roots bind soil), walls/barriers (retaining walls, terraces), and windbreaks (hedges, fences). The core skill is comparing multiple solutions against evidence and judging which works best, ideally via a simple fair comparative test (same slope + same water, different protection). Emphasise there is rarely one 'perfect' answer — solutions have trade-offs and suit different situations — and that a claim ('plants work best') needs EVIDENCE from a test or observation. Keep it concrete and comparative, not a lecture on erosion mechanisms.
bestPractices: Ground the problem first: show wind/water carrying soil away, so the solutions have a purpose.
COMPARE at least two or three solutions (plants, barriers/walls, windbreaks) rather than studying one — comparison is the learning target.
Judge solutions from EVIDENCE — a simple fair test (same slope, same water, different protection) or observation — not opinion.
Surface trade-offs: no single solution is always best; which wins depends on the situation (slope, wind vs water, cost/effort).
Have children make and defend a claim about which solution works best, citing their evidence.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side test trays: bare soil vs planted vs walled, same water poured.
A solutions comparison chart (solution → how it helps → how well it worked).
Before/after images of a slope with and without protection.
Model barriers: mini retaining wall, plant roots, windbreak hedge.
commonMisconceptions: 'One solution is always best' — not seeing that the right choice depends on the situation and trade-offs.
'Plants cause erosion / plants are just decoration' — not recognising roots bind and hold soil.
'Walls stop all erosion forever' — overlooking that barriers can fail, overtop, or shift.
'You can just decide which is best by looking' — skipping the fair test/evidence.
'Wind and water erosion need the same solution' — windbreaks vs water barriers suit different agents.

learn.summary: For 7\u20138 year olds comparing engineering solutions that slow or prevent wind and [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-1]. The core target is COMPARING two or three solutions (plants/ground cover, barriers/walls, windbreaks) against EVIDENCE from a simple fair test \u2014 not opinion \u2014 and defending a claim about which works best, while recognising trade-offs and that the best choice depends on the situation.

activities.title: Erosion-defence fair test: bare vs planted vs walled
feedback: If a winner is announced before testing: ask 'how could we check?' and require pointing to what was observed before deciding.
If water amount or pour height varies between trays: model controlling variables \u2014 keep everything the same except the solution being tested, then re-run.
If the choice isn't tied to what happened: ask which tray's catch tray held the most soil and how that was seen or measured.
activities.rationale: The standard is to compare multiple solutions and judge from evidence; a side-by-side test where the learner applies different protections to identical slopes, delivers the same water, and reads the soil saved makes the comparison evidence-based rather than asserted. An interactive bench with a 'storm' control and a soil-loss meter under each slope makes the comparison mechanism concrete; a real soil-tray comparison with a watering can is a strong hands-on version. These interface details are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Vegetation/ground cover, barriers (retaining walls, terraces) and windbreaks reduce erosion by binding soil or blocking the eroding agent; solutions have trade-offs and suit different conditions.
learnerActions: First watch or recall how wind and water carry soil away from a slope, so the solutions have a clear purpose.

Set up three identical sloped trays of soil: one bare, one covered with living ground cover such as grass/moss (the cover shields the soil surface and roots, where present, bind it), one backed by a small retaining wall.
Pour the SAME amount of water from the SAME height over each tray, and catch the runoff/soil in a tray beneath each.

Measure or compare how much soil each slope lost (e.g. read a soil-loss catch tray or meter) and rank the three trays from least to most soil lost, using the bare tray as the no-protection comparison.
Name which solution worked best and point to the evidence you saw or measured to justify it.
State what you kept the same (water amount, pour height, slope) to make it a fair test.
Design and drop in your OWN barrier and test it the same way.
activities.intendedInsight: You judge which solution works best from evidence in a fair comparative test \u2014 keeping everything the same except the solution \u2014 rather than deciding by belief or by guessing from how a solution looks before testing.

activities.title: Which solution for THIS situation? Surfacing trade-offs
feedback: If one solution is applied to every case without reasoning: contrast a wind case with a water case, and discuss why plant roots hold soil and why a wall can overtop.
If 'a wall always works' appears: point out barriers can fail, overtop, or shift, and ask what evidence would show that.
If cost/effort is ignored: prompt comparison of how much effort each solution takes against how much soil it saves.
activities.rationale: Comparing solutions across differing agents and sites targets the trade-off reasoning the standard requires and directly addresses the 'one solution is always best' and 'a wall always works' misconceptions. An in-role engineer or farmer persona that asks the learner to defend a choice and weigh cost/effort can prompt evaluation and argument-from-evidence; a discussion alone does not generate the test measurements, so pair it with the fair test.
sourceClaims: Vegetation/ground cover, barriers (retaining walls, terraces) and windbreaks reduce erosion by binding soil or blocking the eroding agent; solutions have trade-offs and suit different conditions.
learnerActions: Compare a rainy slope scenario with a windy flat field scenario.

Decide which solution suits each situation: e.g. a windbreak (hedge/fence) to slow wind on the flat field, or a wall on a water slope \u2014 noting that plants/ground cover help reduce BOTH wind and water erosion because their roots bind the soil and the cover shields the surface.
Explain why one solution can beat another when the situation changes (water pooling/overtopping a wall, roots binding soil, wind vs water).
Consider cost/effort trade-offs for a site (e.g. 'the wall costs more \u2014 is it worth it here?') and justify your pick.
activities.intendedInsight: There is rarely one perfect solution: the best choice depends on the situation (slope vs flat, wind vs water, cost/effort), and solutions have trade-offs; some solutions (like ground cover/plants) can help against more than one agent.

activities.title: Reading and organising the comparison evidence
feedback: If plants are seen as decoration or as causing erosion: show that roots bind and hold soil in place and ground cover shields the surface.
If the chart is misread: re-read the soil-lost column and compare the numbers directly.
Recognition and sorting support vocabulary but do not themselves show a learner can run and interpret a fair test \u2014 pair with the hands-on comparison.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching, sequencing and chart-reading reinforce the solution-to-mechanism vocabulary and let learners interpret comparison evidence cleanly. These recognition-style tasks assess and consolidate understanding but do not elicit the independent test-design and evidence generation that defines the node, so they complement rather than replace the fair test.
sourceClaims: Vegetation/ground cover, barriers (retaining walls, terraces) and windbreaks reduce erosion by binding soil or blocking the eroding agent; solutions have trade-offs and suit different conditions.
learnerActions: Match each solution to how it helps (plants/roots \u2192 bind and hold soil, and the cover shields the surface; wall/terrace \u2192 block or hold back soil and water; windbreak \u2192 slow the wind).
Sort solutions by which eroding agent(s) they suit, remembering some solutions help against more than one.
Read a results chart (solution \u2192 how it helps \u2192 how much soil lost) and identify which slope lost the least soil.
Build a comparison chart from your own test results and use it to defend your claim.
activities.intendedInsight: Organising results into a comparison (solution \u2192 mechanism \u2192 how well it worked) lets you reason clearly about which solution wins and why.

constraints: Ground the problem first: show wind/water carrying soil away so solutions have a purpose, before comparing them.
Compare at least two or three solutions (plants, barriers/walls, windbreaks); studying only one misses the learning target.

Judgements must come from evidence \u2014 a fair test (same slope, same water amount, same pour height) or careful observation of what happened \u2014 not opinion or a quick guess from how a solution looks before testing.
Keep it concrete and comparative; avoid a lecture on erosion mechanisms.
Do not pin each eroding agent to a single fixed solution: ground cover/plants reduce both wind and water erosion, and the point is situation-dependence, not a one-to-one rule.
Recognition/sorting/chart-reading tasks consolidate vocabulary and can assess understanding, but do not by themselves elicit independent fair-test design or evidence generation.
A persona/discussion can prompt justification and trade-off reasoning but does not produce the comparative test measurements; pair it with an actual test.
Tap-to-reveal static scenes build recognition and vocabulary but a learner cannot manipulate variables or generate evidence from them; use as a scaffold alongside testing.
Physical soil trays have real material behaviour; screen models are idealised approximations of the same comparison \u2014 treat screen outputs as a model, not a measurement of real soil.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Legacy entries asserted that static art 'can't deliver' compare-from-evidence and that a persona 'can't run the comparative test', and ranked 3D as 'heavier/adds nothing' for this age. These are reframed here as scoped affordances/limits, not universal laws \u2014 a fixed scene or a 3D slope can still teach recognition or spatial aspects; comparative necessity of the 2D bench is not established by the sources.

The real-world claim that 'the windbreak beats the wall' on a windy flat field is plausible but depends on specific materials and setup; it is presented as a scenario to reason about and test, not a guaranteed outcome.

Ground cover/plants reduce both wind and water erosion; the original recommendation's wording occasionally implied agent-specific solutions, which was corrected to avoid reinforcing the 'different agents always need different solutions' misconception.

Soil-loss 'meters' and 'soil-saved' numbers from the legacy recommendation are interface illustrations; outcomes in a real tray depend on soil type, slope and water volume and should be measured, not assumed.

The diagnostic's 'grass/moss' example is retained, but moss anchors by rhizoids rather than true roots; the ground-cover wording was scoped so the root-binding mechanism is claimed only where roots are present, while the surface-shielding benefit covers both.

probeDeeper: What did you keep the same for each tray so the test was fair?
Which tray lost the most soil, and how could you see that?
This test used water. Would the same solution be best against wind? Why might it differ?
If you ran the test again, would you get the same result? How could you be more sure?
assess.correctAnswer: The child pours equally over each tray, observes that the bare soil washes away most while the planted or walled slopes hold more soil, and concludes which solution worked best — citing what they saw and having kept the water amount and height the same (a fair test).

errorPatterns.pattern: Picks the winner before testing, from belief not evidence ('plants always win')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'how could we check?' and require them to point to what they saw before deciding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Announces the best solution without running or referring to the test.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unfair test — pours different amounts or from different heights, then compares the trays
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model controlling variables — keep everything the same except the solution being tested.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Varies the water volume or pour height between trays.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any barrier stops erosion regardless of how water or wind moves ('a wall always works')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a wind case with a water case, and discuss why plant roots hold soil in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies one solution to every case without considering water pooling/overtopping or wind vs water.

responseLevels.gap: Declares a best solution without testing, or runs an unfair comparison and can't say what happened.
responseLevels.full: Runs a fair test (same water, same height), observes the outcomes, and justifies the best solution from that evidence — recognising the right solution depends on how wind or water acts on the land.
responseLevels.partial: Runs the test and names a winner, but doesn't control the variables or doesn't tie the choice to observed evidence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three trays of sloped soil, plus pieces of grass/moss, a small wall, and a bare tray. Pour the same cup of water over each from the same height, then tell me which lost the least soil and use what you saw to say which solution works best and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who 'knows plants stop erosion' as a fact may name a winner before testing or pour unequal amounts. Watching shows whether they actually generate and use evidence from a controlled comparison rather than reciting a belief — which is the design-comparison claim being assessed.
